title: Unit – 2 : Session – 5 : SLO – 2 | Memory Operations and Byte Addressing
sections: Section A – Match the Following (Answers)
1. Load Operation → E. Memory read from a specified address
2. Store Operation → B. Memory write from processor to specified location
3. Big-Endian → D. Most significant byte stored at lowest address
4. Little-Endian → A. Least significant byte stored at lowest address
5. 32-bit Data Alignment → C. Word starts at byte address 0, 4, 8…
Section B – Fill in the Blanks
The LOAD operation reads the contents of a specified memory location.
The STORE operation stores processor data into a specific memory location.
In BIG-ENDIAN representation, the most significant byte is stored at the lowest memory address.
In LITTLE-ENDIAN representation, the least significant byte is stored at the lowest memory address.
In 64-bit data alignment, words begin at byte addresses such as 0, 8, 16, and so on.
Section C – Activity Task
Task 1 – Word 0x46789654 stored at address 8000h:

Task 2a – Why endianness matters: machines that use different byte orders interpret the same binary sequence differently; when binary data is transferred between systems the byte order must be agreed or converted, otherwise multi-byte values are read incorrectly.

Task 2b – Aligned vs unaligned access: an aligned word starts at an address that is a multiple of its size (e.g. 0, 4, 8 for 4-byte words) and is fetched in one memory cycle; an unaligned word straddles two word boundaries, needing multiple accesses and extra merging logic, so it is slower and on some architectures not permitted.
Section D – True or False
In Big-endian format, the most significant byte is stored last. — FALSE (it is stored at the lowest address)
Aligned 16-bit words begin at addresses like 0, 2, 4… — TRUE
Little-endian format is commonly used in Intel processors. — TRUE
A load operation writes data to memory. — FALSE (load reads memory; store writes)
Word alignment helps in faster memory access and avoids errors in some architectures. — TRUE
